Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes hypervigilance, startle, danger in silence, fragmented/avoided trauma memory, and appraisals of betrayal and injustice after police violence. Those other items describe a fearful, threat-sensitive presentation; endorsing active risk-taking as a core threat item pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported elsewhere in the selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself
issues.explanation: 'Can't Rely on Self' is a weaker fit than the other appraisals for this trauma/context. The profile is organized around external betrayal/injustice linked to police violence, but this item shifts to global self-distrust without corresponding self-blame, shame, incompetence, or strategy items elsewhere. In combination with the strong betrayal/injustice theme, it creates a less coherent appraisal profile.

vignette: On a gray Tuesday in early spring, Miguel, a 54‑year‑old parole officer of Puerto Rican descent, found himself in the middle of a chaotic morning shift at the downtown parole center. A client, visibly agitated, began to throw a tantrum that threatened to erupt into a fight with the staff. Miguel called the police to manage the situation, and within seconds the officers arrived, brandishing batons and shouting commands. In a split second, a gunshot‑like crack of a rubber bullet rang through the corridor, and Miguel felt his heart pound so hard it seemed to beat outside his chest. He watched the officers physically assault the client, who was clearly compliant, and the scene unfolded as a stark moral violation—people misbehaving in a place meant for safety. The moral violation immediately triggered a sense of threat; the sudden violence made the air feel charged, as if danger lurked in the silence that followed the last shout. Miguel’s heart racing reinforced his belief that something dangerous was about to happen again. This threat in silence, combined with his tendency to be startled at even the slightest noise, forced him to scan his surroundings with a hyper‑vigilant eye. The same scene also triggered negative appraisals: he felt betrayed by those who were meant to protect him, convinced that the event was an injustice, and harbored a conviction that the institutions—law enforcement and the parole system—had let him down. These judgments were not fleeting; they were the lens through which the whole episode was refracted. Because Miguel carried the weight of betrayal, injustice, and institutional failure, his memory of the event became fractured. He found himself repeatedly trying to pull the narrative together, only to realize he could not fully recall the sequence; the memory felt blocked before it was complete. The story also seemed unreal, as if it had been filmed and then played back from a distance, and the pieces he remembered never coalesced into a coherent picture. The sense of betrayal and the belief that no one had intervened to stop the officers’ excesses amplified his sensitivity to similar moral violations; the more he felt betrayed, the more he became attuned to any instance of misbehaving people, turning the environment of his workplace into a constant trigger. When Miguel later revisited the event in his mind, the incomplete memory acted as a threat trigger. The gaps in the narrative left room for fear—what if something else had happened, what if the memory was wrong? This perception of an unfinished story amplified his sense of injustice, reinforcing the belief that the system had failed him. The memory’s unreal quality deepened the emotional charge, reminding him that the injustice was real even if the details were hazy. His incomplete recollection, combined with the heightened threat of missing something, created a feedback loop that made each recollection feel both threatening and deeply unjust. The ongoing sense of threat, in turn, pulled Miguel back into his memories. The constant vigilance—every sudden creak or quiet pause—sparked intrusive images of the officers’ baton striking the client, and these flashes were accompanied by the same feelings of betrayal and institutional failure he had first felt that day. Each threat cue strengthened his negative appraisals: every new startle response felt like a reminder that the injustice was still present, that the police were still powerful enough to harm. The threat amplified his triggers: seeing another client misbehaving on his shift or hearing a colleague’s whisper about a pending arrest made him feel the same moral violation, and the cycle tightened, each component pulling the others closer together. Miguel finally stepped into therapy after months of feeling the weight of that first violent encounter. He was terrified that each day in his parole office would trigger another wave of heart pounding, startle, and the gnawing belief that he was being betrayed by those who should have protected him. What frightened him most was the realization that his life had been hijacked by a single traumatic moment that now colored every interaction. He hopes that, with help, he can untangle the web of memory, threat, and negative beliefs so that he might reclaim his days from the relentless vigilance that keeps him trapped in a loop he no longer wishes to live in.
